text: I bet you a hundred dollars you can't guess what was illegal in Iceland until 1989.
Not guns, not gambling, beer!
For 74 years beer was banned, while wine and vodka were totally fine.
And that's the normal fact!
This country has a burger that refuses to rot!
An island so new, only scientists are allowed to walk on it.
And a volcano that shut down the skies of an entire continent!
Every single one is real and they get crazier as we go.
Grab a map of Iceland. Here are 8 facts nobody believes, starting with number 8.
Number 8. In Iceland, you can't just name your baby anything.
There's an official list of approved names.
If both parents are Icelandic, the baby's first name has to come from that list.
Want something new? You have to apply to the Naming Committee.
And they can say no.
Over the years, they've rejected names like Harriet, Duncan, and Zoe.
Part of the reason? The Icelandic alphabet doesn't even have the letter C.
And there are no family surnames either.
Your last name is just your dad's or your mom's first name plus son or dóttir.
So a whole country without surnames.
But that's nothing compared to what Iceland didn't have until last year.
7. For all of human history, Iceland had no mosquitoes.
None. Zero.
Along with Antarctica, it was one of the only places on Earth without a single one living there.
Then, in October 2025, an insect collector north of Reykjavik found something strange in his trap.
Three mosquitoes! The first ones ever recorded in Iceland's wild.
So now, Antarctica is believed to be the last mosquito-free place on the planet.
And if you think a bug arriving is strange, wait till you hear what left.
6. Iceland has no McDonald's.
All three restaurants closed in 2009 when the country's economy crashed.
On the very last day, a man named Hjortur Småresen bought one last burger and fries,
just to see if it would ever rot.
Years later, he opened the bag, and it looked almost exactly the same.
Today, that meal sits in a glass case at a guesthouse in South Iceland.
It even got its own live stream so the whole world could watch it, not rot.
A burger frozen in time!
And speaking of things that stay warm, Iceland has a very hot secret.
Number 5. Iceland heats its homes with volcanoes.
Well, with the heat underneath them.
Boiling water from deep underground is piped straight into houses.
Around 90% of Icelandic homes are heated this way.
No gas, no oil.
In parts of Reykjavik, the same hot water runs under the sidewalks, so the snow
just melts.
And almost all of the country's electricity comes from renewable sources, rivers and
steam.
So the ground is literally keeping Iceland warm.
Which is good news for everyone living there, including the ones you can't see.
4. In Iceland, elves can stop a road.
Folk stories say hidden people live in rocks and hills, and many Icelanders take those stories seriously.
A few years ago, a new road was planned through an old lava field near Reykjavik, right through a rock believed to be an elf church.
After years of protests, the road went ahead, but the rock wasn't destroyed.
In 2015, it was carefully lifted and moved so the elves could keep their church.
And just last year, Iceland's road authorities said a bridge project went ahead only after the island's elves approved it.
Elves blocking roads is strange, but in number three, the ground itself is splitting apart.
3. Iceland sits right on top of the crack between two continents.
The North American plate and the Eurasian plate are pulling apart, about 2 centimeters every single year.
So Iceland is slowly stretching.
And at a place called Silfra, that crack is filled with crystal clear glacier water.
You can actually swim in it, one hand touching America's plate, the other touching Europe's.
The water is just 2 to 4 degrees, but it's so clear, it feels like flying.
Continents being made in real time.
And number 2 is a piece of land that didn't exist when your grandparents were born.
Number 2.
In November 1963, fishermen off Iceland's south coast saw smoke rising out of the sea.
A volcano was erupting 130 meters under the water.
The next day, a brand new island appeared!
They named it Surtsey, after a fire giant from Norse myth,
and it kept erupting for almost four years.
But here's the crazy part.
Almost nobody is allowed to visit.
Since 1965, only a few scientists can land there
to study how life arrives on a brand new piece of earth.
No tourists, no sheep, not even a stray seed from your shoes.
An island too young for people.
And number one is the day Iceland made the whole of Europe stop.
Number one.
In April 2010, a volcano erupted under a glacier with a name almost nobody can say.
Eyjafjallajökull.
It wasn't even a giant eruption, but the ash shot about nine kilometers into the sky.
And the wind blew it straight towards Europe.
Volcanic ash can destroy jet engines, so country after country closed its airspace.
More than 300 airports shut down.
Around 100,000 flights were canceled in about a week.
Up to 10 million passengers were stuck.
Some took trains, buses, even taxis across the continent to get home.
It was the biggest shutdown of European air travel since World War II.
Oh, one small country, one volcano,
and the whole sky went quiet.
